HiFloat4 (HiF4) employs a hierarchical scale encoding scheme consisting of a global E6M2 scale and two levels of binary scale extensions. However, its conventional rounding rule and fixed scale extension thresholds may not fully capture the statistical characteristics of the quantized tensors in practice, leading to suboptimal scale representations. In this work, we propose HiCal, an offline calibration approach that improves HiF4 quantization accuracy by refining the encoding decisions across all three scale levels. Specifically, we introduce a calibrated rounding bias for the Level-1 E6M2 scale and optimize the scale-extension thresholds at Levels 2 and 3 based on the empirical distributions of local group magnitudes. The resulting calibration parameters are determined offline and remain fixed during inference, while the hierarchical encoding continues to adapt to individual blocks through their local values. This design eliminates the need for per-block multi-candidate scale search while preserving the original deterministic HiF4 encoding procedure. Experiments across five synthetic and real activation distributions show that the proposed method reduces quantization MSE by 9.91%-23.50% relative to the original HiF4 scheme, including a 13.00% reduction on real Qwen3-8B activations. End-to-end evaluations across six benchmarks further show average-score improvements of 0.91 and 1.25 percentage points on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, respectively, without per-block multi-candidate search during inference.
title: HiCal: Offline Calibration for Hierarchical Scale Encoding in Accurate HiF4 Quantization

abstract: Most information sought online by Twi (Akan) speakers is written in English, making cross-lingual retrieval essential. We evaluate eight systems: BM25, five open embedding models, and two proprietary models (gemini-embedding-001 and OpenAI text-embedding-3-large) on two Twi-English tasks. AfriQA contains 1,221 natively written Asante Twi questions that must retrieve their answering English Wikipedia passages. Bible translation retrieval requires a Twi passage to retrieve its English translation from 6,195 candidates. We introduce MargEmbed-Akan, a 560M-parameter open query encoder trained from AfriE5-Large-instruct using cross-lingual score distillation. The frozen base model scores each English training question against its answer passage and seven hard negatives. The student learns to reproduce these scores from both an NLLB-200 Twi translation that passes a round-trip translation check and the original English question, preserving English behaviour. During training, passages are encoded by the frozen base model; at evaluation, MargEmbed-Akan encodes questions and passages. On AfriQA, base AfriE5 and gemini-embedding-001 both achieve 66.6 nDCG@10; EmbeddingGemma 2, Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B, and OpenAI text-embedding-3-large achieve 56.6, 51.3, and 53.4, respectively. MargEmbed-Akan achieves 71.5, outperforming gemini-embedding-001 by 4.9 points, its base model by 5.0, and OpenAI text-embedding-3-large by 18.1. Its largest gain is on Twi typed without E and O (+7.5 over gemini-embedding-001). English retrieval does not differ significantly from the base model, although both proprietary models score 1.5-2.2 points higher. On Bible translation retrieval, MargEmbed-Akan and gemini-embedding-001 are statistically tied on standard Twi (97.2 vs. 96.5 nDCG@10); MargEmbed-Akan performs better on diacritic-free Twi (92.7 vs. 84.9). No AfriQA data was used for training or model selection.
title: MargEmbed-Akan: Bridging Twi Questions and English Knowledge through Cross-Lingual Score Distillation

abstract: Training or evaluating a model that turns a conversation into a structured record requires paired data, meaning a transcript together with the exact record it should be converted into. Such pairs are expensive to annotate, and in sensitive domains they are also difficult to obtain at all. We therefore build them in the opposite order by sampling a schema-valid record first, then writing a dialogue from it, and optionally synthesizing speech from the dialogue, so the label exists before the text and we need no annotation step. Naively prompting a language model for such dialogues yields small variations of a single conversation, so we add a sampled variation configuration, personas, and a topic plan that orders the fields of the record as explicit mechanisms for variation. We measure the variation that reaches the output through embedding space, where the embedding variance spreads over about two and a half times as many independent directions with our full configuration compared to without (participation ratio 23.3 against 9.2). Two corpora of medical dialogue give values of the same order, with sample size, text length and language being additional factors there. We also show the positive effect of our method in a downstream test, where an 8B extraction model reaches 64.8% field accuracy when fine-tuned on dialogues from our method, against 57.5% from naive generation. We release the generation library and the generated corpus of German clinical dialogues with aligned records.
title: Generating Schema-Aligned Synthetic Dialogues and Measuring Their Diversity

abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) enables vision-language-action policies to improve through environmental interaction. However, in long-horizon manipulation, sparse success/failure feedback provides little information about where policies encounter bottlenecks. Moreover, repeated full-task rollouts also leave these bottlenecks weakly analyzed and insufficiently practiced. To this end, we introduce ReFocus, a progress-guided multi-round RL framework that alternates between Global and Local RL to identify task-specific bottlenecks and allocate additional practice to them. Specifically, during Global RL, we decompose each task into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of subtasks. Then a DAG-based Progress Reward is leveraged for both policy training and bottleneck diagnosis. Based on the identified bottlenecks, ReFocus selects Adaptive Practice Windows, defining task segments from an entry stage to a target stage. It allocates additional interaction to these segments during Local RL while updating the entire policy. After that, it evaluates the policy to perform the full task for the next round of RL, forming an iteration between Global and Local RL. Experiments on LIBERO-Long and RoboCasa365 show that ReFocus achieves success rates of 97.8% and 51.3%, respectively, compared with 90.6% and 39.3% for the $π_{0.5}$ baseline. Furthermore, we evaluate a real-world adaptation on three long-horizon tasks. On BreadBaker, ReFocus achieves 95% success, compared with 30% for the $π_{0.5}$. Project page: https://refocus-robotics.github.io.
title: ReFocus: Progress-Guided Adaptive Practice for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Dynamic obstacle avoidance is essential for safely deploying humanoid robots in real-world environments, where rapidly approaching objects require immediate evasive responses. Recent advances in reflexive evasion have focused primarily on quadrupeds, which typically rely on large-scale whole-body maneuvers. In contrast, humanoids can exploit their rich body articulation to evade through small, localized body adjustments. By moving threatened body regions without repositioning the entire body, these responses may require less execution time and less surrounding free space. However, local adjustments can alter mass distribution or support conditions, making it challenging to achieve rapid evasion while maintaining whole-body stability. To this end, we propose BARE (Body-Aware Reflexive Evasion), a humanoid reflexive evasion framework guided by human motion priors that enables rapid local evasion while maintaining whole-body stability. A risk-guided motion adapter is designed to select reference motions from a retargeted human evasive motion library based on the threatened body region and to adjust their temporal phases based on collision urgency, allowing the robot to reach evasive postures before potential contact. Conditioned on the adapted reference and link-level collision risk, a reflexive evasion policy learns through reinforcement learning to coordinate local body adjustments with whole-body stabilization. We validate BARE in simulation and real-world experiments, demonstrating its ability to perform targeted local evasion while maintaining whole-body stability.
title: BARE: Body-Aware Reflexive Evasion for Humanoid Robots

abstract: Complex cooperative tasks require coordinated multi-agent behavior. Offline generative policies learn expressive cooperative behaviors from trajectories but remain limited by fixed datasets. Online reinforcement learning can improve them through environment interaction. However, fine-tuning flow policies is difficult because action likelihoods are hard to compute. We propose TeamFlowRL, a two-stage framework that pretrains multi-agent flow policies offline and fine-tunes them online. We formulate team policy optimization over the complete denoising trajectories of decentralized flow policies, avoiding intractable action likelihoods. The resulting objective weights each agent's trajectory ratio with a shared team advantage and clips each ratio separately, aligning local policy updates with the common team return. Across 51 paired configurations in seven simulation groups, TeamFlowRL improves every offline initialization, with a 47.3% average gain in normalized score. It also achieves 33.1% higher average success under exploration noise than Gaussian-policy fine-tuning across 6 bimanual tasks.
title: TeamFlowRL: Online Policy Optimization of Decentralized Flow Policies for Multi-Agent Coordination

abstract: Official statistics are critical datasets for a wide variety of actors, including policymakers and businesses. For providers of official statistics, improving accessibility, governance, and disclosure of their data is of key importance. This can be improved by providing question-answering systems based on text-to-SQL approaches. However, existing text-to-SQL benchmarks do not resemble this setting. Official statistics are published as open-domain catalogs of thousands of wide tables whose columns and values are codes, and whose meaning is recorded in separate metadata rather than in a relational schema. To address this gap, we introduce LOCuST, a text-to-SQL benchmark that pairs over two thousand English and Dutch tables from Statistics Netherlands with a semantic knowledge graph. The graph describes the tables, measures, and dimension codes through labels, definitions, hierarchies, and units, and is the external knowledge a system needs to find the right tables and ground a question in the right codes. The benchmark includes expert-annotated questions for different query and aggregation types, including raw value retrieval, summations, proportion calculations, and joins. Alongside standard evaluation measures, we introduce an observation F1 metric that measures how close a query is to the ground truth even when the answers are different. We evaluate a variety of state-of-the-art LLMs and find that they struggle to write SQL that answers the questions correctly.
title: A Text-to-SQL Benchmark for Official Statistics

abstract: In-context learning (ICL) lets agents acquire new rules from context and adapt to user-specific requirements at inference time. The same frontier agents now operate both computers and robots, yet their ICL remains insufficiently assessed: existing benchmarks are largely offline, rely on text or static images, and risk training-data contamination, while robot evaluations are limited to method-level ablations. We present ICLWorld, an online benchmark that evaluates the ICL of agents from digital to physical worlds, covering computer use and robot use, together with UIverse, a unified harness that turns every environment into a user interface. We build 30 environments, record 630 demonstration videos (10+ hours), and design 160 tasks with customized, often counter-intuitive rules that cannot be satisfied without learning from the context. Each task comes with three rule versions, given as text or video, and we test generalization at three levels, from replaying the demonstration to new instances and unseen environments. Across six frontier models, the strongest agents, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, succeed on 82% and 76% of computer-use runs but only 27% and 26% of robot-use runs, and a no-rule control reduces success to at most 8%. GPT-6 Astra succeeds under all three rule versions on only 38% of computer-use tasks, half its rate under a single rule, and answers 98% of robot rule questions correctly yet completes only 20% of these tasks. Frontier agents learn rules comparably well from video and from text and transfer them across environments, whereas weaker agents rely on text and lose most of their video-based success once the demonstrated situation is resampled. These findings reveal substantial gaps between the digital and the physical world and between identifying a rule and acting on it.
title: ICLWorld: Benchmarking In-Context Learning of Agents from Digital to Physical Worlds

abstract: With the growing scale of scientific simulation and infrastructure, part of the burden has shifted from producing scientific data to analyzing and storing it. Compression is a key step to expanding storage capacity, but requires dedicated techniques to enforce user-specified pointwise error bounds that ensure the validity of downstream scientific workflows. To further push the limits of compression, novel learned codecs have been developed, in particular for images and videos, but these methods often optimize for aggregated distortion and fail to meet error bound standards. Moreover, these methods often target fixed field dimensionality, failing to account for many scientific data use cases, or at the expense of large adaptation or retraining costs. In this work, we introduce the Learned Axial TEnsor Compression (LATEC) method, an error-bounded codec with a dimension-agnostic learned predictor based on a GNN architecture. LATEC is pretrained on synthetic 2-D and 4-D fields, and evaluated with and without domain fine-tuning on 13 scientific fields in 3-D to 5-D. Results show that LATEC is consistently competitive with SZ3, achieving an 18.1% average improvement and greater consistency across all domains than other compressors. These results demonstrate that a shared learned predictor can serve as a single error-bounded codec across tensor dimensionalities, competitive with specialized compressors, while retaining pointwise error guarantees.
title: LATEC: Learned Axial TEnsor Compression for High-Dimensional Scientific Data

abstract: Robot demonstrations provide more than actions to imitate: they reveal how actions change the world and how those changes contribute to task success. Recent world-action models (WAMs) extend vision-language-action (VLA) models with the first signal by jointly predicting actions and future observations, yet this predictive ability serves only as an auxiliary loss for policy learning. Meanwhile, most policy improvement methods learn dynamics and values in separate models, increasing training overhead and limiting representation sharing between these complementary objectives. We introduce DexWAC, a unified world-actor-critic model that jointly learns an actor, an action-conditioned world model, and a bootstrapped critic in a single robot pretraining stage. Our key insight is that visual prediction encourages control-relevant features, while value supervision promotes task-relevant representations; together, they shape a representation suited to policy learning. Built on an image-editing backbone, DexWAC predicts, for each action chunk, the visual latent and proprioception at its endpoint together with its reward and continuation, so the world model alone efficiently yields complete imagined transitions without generating intermediate video frames. After adapting the world model and critic on real rollouts, we improve the pretrained actor through either PPO on imagined rollouts or critic-guided best-of-$N$ selection. DexWAC surpasses the large-scale pretrained VLA and WAM baselines in simulation and achieves 75% average success on two real-world tasks, compared with 45% for $π_{0.5}$. Its world model is more accurate and faster than video-based baselines, and ablations confirm that learning dynamics and value together improves the policy.
title: DexWAC: A Unified World-Actor-Critic Model for Dexterous Robot Manipulation

abstract: Surgical resection planning centers on generating executable resection surfaces from anatomical evidence and operative constraints. Medical multimodal foundation models enable anatomical understanding, and segmentation models predict resection regions, but neither translates these capabilities into explicitly constrained, executable resection surfaces. We present GeoSurge, an anatomy-grounded framework that combines mask-derived metrics with structure-aware point-cloud tokens to generate executable, editable resection surfaces. To make resection geometry learnable and editable, GeoSurge maps actions to parametric geometry through a surface-action grammar. Using this grammar, anatomy-oriented and tumor-centered templates generate candidates, which are filtered by hard constraints and semantic deduplication. Training supervision is then derived from candidate-expert geometric agreement and independently recomputed feasibility metrics. At inference, the reasoner uses patient evidence and surgical requirements to select or revise an action, which an independent geometry engine subsequently materializes and verifies. GeoSurge achieves the best overall scores on DeepTumour Liver and CRLM-QA, improving the constraint satisfaction rate from 73% to 100% on CRLM and from 56% to 99% on GeoSurge-Bench.
title: GeoSurge: Geometry-Grounded Multimodal Reasoning for Auditable Liver Resection Planning

abstract: Deep search is a critical capability for agents tackling complex, open-ended tasks, where solving a problem requires iterative information gathering, query reformulation, and evidence-based verification rather than a single retrieval step. To address these requirements, we present Bathys 9B and 27B deep search agents built around a training framework that spans verifiable question synthesis, post-training, and online reinforcement learning (RL) under context compression. Our high-quality data construction ensures both search depth and reliability: each clue is reformulated as an indirect reference requiring independent retrieval, and retained evidence chains enable verification that the clues jointly determine a unique answer. Curated trajectories underpin a pipeline of supervised fine-tuning (SFT), Kahneman-Tversky Optimization (KTO), and Compaction-Managed Group Sequence Policy Optimization (CM-GSPO): SFT provides a stable foundation for tool use over long horizons and query reformulation; KTO uses binary feedback on trajectories to improve the selection of answers grounded in evidence; CM-GSPO optimizes execution sub-trajectories with length-normalized likelihood ratios on the recorded rollout contexts and reweights sub-trajectory advantages to correct the extra weighting introduced by independently averaging sub-trajectory losses. Bathys 9B and 27B attain 66.51% and 80.49% on BrowseComp, respectively, under an evaluation protocol with trajectory self-verification and conditional retries.
title: Bathys: Advancing Deep Search Agents

abstract: Online Machine Learning (ML) enables real-time decision-making on evolving data streams. These dynamic models learn continuously to adapt to new concepts, as previous ones become invalid, but their performance is often limited by throughput. The Adaptive Random Forest (ARF) is a state-of-the-art model for this setting, which naturally exposes parallelism and is therefore well-suited for hardware acceleration. However, prior Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA)-based accelerators are vendor-locked and rely on resource-hungry Floating-Point (FP) arithmetics, limiting their scalability and portability. We present OpenWoud, a vendor-unlocked ARF framework for FPGAs. Our design replaces FP operators with a flexible FiXed-Point (FxP) arithmetic library and introduces fully transparent, manually scheduled dataflows for training and drift detection. This enables fine-grained time/area trade-offs and predictable behavior across platforms. A comprehensive evaluation on both synthetic and real datasets shows that OpenWoud maintains or increases accuracy (up to +12.89%), compared to a prior FPGA accelerator, while reducing the resource utilization by half. Competitive performance is observed compared to GPU (0.5 - 1.5x speed-up) and an FPGA baseline (0.2 - 0.5x), despite the latter being based on idealized simulation. Crucially, OpenWoud sustains true sample-by-sample inference, unlike GPUs that require batch insertion.
title: OpenWoud: Vendor-Unlocked Scalable Adaptive Random Forest Accelerator

abstract: Can artificial intelligence reproduce the economic dynamics that emerge as households, firms and governments interact and adapt through markets and institutions? To answer this question, we define an economic world model (EWM) as an agent's internal representation of how an economic system works, enabling counterfactual simulation and decision-making under resource constraints. We then propose a general framework for studying EWMs that links three tasks: simulating agent behaviour, learning economic transitions and systematically evaluating the dynamics. As an initial implementation, we learn household policies from microeconomic data and calibrate a structural economic transition model using macroeconomic data, linking individual decisions to aggregate dynamics. Our micro-to-macro evaluation framework compares simulated individual actions and group distributions with observed microdata and assesses macroeconomic dynamics through forecasting and counterfactual experiments. Results show that simulated and observed household consumption distributions overlap by 94.9%, while EWM forecasts closely track real GDP and several other aggregate levels. In government-borrowing counterfactuals, the EWM reproduces the benchmark life-cycle model's short-run transmission from borrowing to consumption. For ex ante planning, the EWM enables an LLM agent to achieve 10.29% higher simulated GDP under the epidemic shock than direct LLM decisions. This initial EWM is only a starting point. We invite economists and AI researchers to build a stronger EWM together. Economists can contribute richer economic models and knowledge, while AI researchers can develop stronger data-driven methods for simulating agent behaviour and learning economic transitions. Together, we aim not only to reproduce real economic dynamics, but also to discover and test new mechanisms that support better decisions and benefit society.
title: Economic World Model

abstract: Multilingual models exhibit social bias when processing inputs pertaining to societal stereotypes. We adapt emerging mechanistic interpretability methods to pinpoint and characterize model components that encode this bias. We conduct our analysis across three instruction-tuned models, four languages, and seven bias dimensions. Specifically, we leverage multilingual bias benchmarks in implementing two methods for identifying social bias neurons: activation probability entropy and integrated gap gradients. We find the latter method to be more effective, as the neurons it isolates (which are largely concentrated at the model's deepest layers) lead to sharper decreases in model bias when suppressed. Further analysis reveals neuron distribution patterns differ between high- and low-resourced languages, suggesting that a language's representation in pretraining data influences how its biases are represented within model internals. Our results also indicate that neurons linked to gender, nationality, and social class biases overlap the most with neurons related to other bias dimensions, pointing to the pivotal role these three dimensions play in how models learn and handle bias.
title: Social Bias Neurons in Multilingual Language Models: A Mechanistic Interpretability Analysis

abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents access remote services through tools to complete user tasks, often via API calls. In this setting, a remote service may want to identify the backend LLM of an agent to launch model-specific attacks, including prompt injection or selective delivery of manipulated content. However, the service cannot directly query the backend model and must instead collect observable responses through its interactions with the agent, making identification challenging. In this paper, we present Completely Automated Preference Test to tell LLMs Apart (CAPTA), a model identification approach inspired by CAPTCHA (Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart), which distinguishes humans from automated programs. CAPTA presents multiple-choice questions as verification challenges, using differences in models' selection preferences to identify the backend LLM. It selects questions based on cross-model option-generation diversity and uses LLM-guided search to optimize their option sets. Our evaluation shows that CAPTA achieves 99.0% mean identification accuracy with only 10 questions across 25 LLMs from 10 model families. We further evaluate CAPTA with four widely used agents and seven representative LLMs, achieving 99.7% mean identification accuracy across all 28 agent-LLM combinations with 30 submitted answers.
title: CAPTA: Identifying LLMs Behind AI Agents

abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) based on Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has been widely adopted to enhance the multimodal reasoning of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, existing methods share a common limitation of Module-Level Credit Entanglement, in which the vision encoder, projector, and LLM modules are jointly optimized using the same advantage signals even when perceptual correctness and final-answer correctness differ. To address this limitation, we propose Module-Specific Policy Optimization (MSPO), a framework that separates perceptual and outcome-based learning signals across model modules. Specifically, MSPO uses responses to perception checklists comprising auxiliary questions about visual information to derive an advantage for training the vision encoder. From these responses, MSPO computes the Confidence-aware Perception Reward (CaPR), using a perception sign obtained by thresholding checklist accuracy to determine reward direction and posterior confidence from a Beta distribution over latent perception accuracy to scale reward magnitude. We then derive the vision advantage through group-relative normalization of CaPR and scale it using main-task success rates. This advantage guides updates to the vision encoder, while the projector and LLM retain outcome-based GRPO updates. Extensive experiments on seven mathematical and general reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that MSPO outperforms existing RL-tuned models on average at both the 3B and 7B scales.
title: Are We Rewarding the Wrong Module? Module-Specific Policy Optimization for Multimodal Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Neural networks in continual learning often lose plasticity: some neurons become inactive, while others fire almost constantly. This limits adaptation to shifting data and wastes capacity. Prior work mitigates this by periodically reinitializing low-utility units, but such resets can destroy previously learned features and do not proactively prevent low utility. We study a simple diagnostic measure: the firing rate of ReLU units, defined as the fraction of positive pre-activations. Low rates identify dead units, while very high rates indicate linearized, always-on units. Based on this view, we introduce a lightweight load-balancing mechanism that adjusts per-neuron thresholds to keep firing rates within a target range. Across continual ImageNet and class-incremental CIFAR-100, firing-rate distributions explain differences in plasticity across a range of approaches, including well-known techniques such as L2 regularization and non-affine normalization, and load balancing matches or exceeds reset-based methods on both benchmarks. The same mechanism carries over to reinforcement learning, improving Rainbow DQN on Atari over a LayerNorm baseline.
title: Load Balancing Neurons: Firing-Rate Control Sustains Plasticity in Continual Learning

abstract: Fast prediction of radio-wave propagation over irregular terrain is important for coverage analysis in mountainous environments, where many terrain and antenna configurations must be evaluated repeatedly. High-fidelity split-step parabolic equation (SSPE) solvers can capture terrain-induced shadowing and interference, but their computational cost is high for repeated planning studies. Learning-based surrogates reduce this cost, but direct field regression asks the network to learn both analytically tractable propagation trends and terrain-dependent residual structure. This paper proposes a hybrid analytical-neural residual surrogate that separates these two parts. A deterministic analytical baseline represents free-space spreading, antenna directivity, modified knife-edge diffraction, and terrain-aware specular reflection, while a compact coarse-to-fine neural network predicts the residual field. The network uses baseline-derived guidance channels, anisotropic convolutions, and feature-wise antenna conditioning to match the directional structure of terrain propagation fields. On synthetic SSPE data at 1.0 GHz, the proposed model achieves an MAE of 2.1061 dB, compared with 3.3955 dB for a standard U-Net and 3.2560 dB for a reproduced physics-guided CNN, while reducing the average inference time to 11.30 ms per sample. A zero-shot test at 1.8 GHz gives an MAE of 2.8692 dB without retraining, and a case study on the measured Hjorringvej terrain profile shows that the prediction remains consistent with the SSPE reference and follows the measured path-loss trend.
title: A Hybrid Analytical-Neural Residual Surrogate for Fast Radio Propagation Prediction over Irregular Terrain

abstract: Proximal causal inference removes unmeasured confounding using two proxies of the confounder, an outcome-side W and a treatment-side Z. The proxies must satisfy exclusion restrictions and be complete, meaning that they reflect every aspect of the confounder. In practice, they are a few variables hand-picked from a structured table, even though clinical notes and physiological waveforms carry rich information about the confounder. Such records are too high-dimensional for a proximal estimator, and generic compression such as PCA may keep modality-specific variation (style) instead of the confounder, destroying completeness. Our key observation is that, under the proximal condition, the confounder is the only link between a treatment-side and an outcome-side modality beyond the covariates. Learning what they share therefore captures the confounder and filters out modality-specific style. Contrastive Proxy Forests (CPF) learns both proxies by contrasting the two modalities, given the covariates, on a separate unlabeled sample, and passes them to a proximal causal forest. This contrastive objective has an exact closed-form solution, ridge canonical correlation analysis. We prove that CPF preserves the exclusion restrictions exactly and that its proxies inherit the completeness of the raw records under conditions we characterize. Where style is strong, CPF lowers the error of conditional effects by 10-22% relative to PCA proxies, and on MIMIC-IV it is the only method whose point estimate of warfarin's effect on stroke falls inside the range of randomized trials.
title: Contrastive Proxy Forests: Completeness-Preserving Proxy Learning from Multimodal Records

abstract: Open-weight large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed for applications with sensitive information. We investigate whether confidentiality instructions in system prompt can protect such information. We red-team Apertus v1.5, an open sovereign LLM, and five other model families across six languages and reasoning modes. We use synthetic personal records to evaluate direct disclosure, correction baits, yes/no verification, derived-value queries, reasoning leakage and authorisation checks. We also explore copyright attribution, historical misrepresentation and stereotyping. Despite confidentiality instructions, Apertus 8B and 70B leak information in 96% and 95% of requests, respectively, in correction-bait attacks. Verification and derived-value queries also expose protected information without necessarily revealing identifiers. Moreover, reasoning traces can leak confidential records even when final answers withhold them. Our experiments also show that post-training does not consistently improve safety. Our findings demonstrate that system prompts alone cannot ensure confidentiality and highlight the need for multilingual reasoning-aware safety evaluations.
title: Red-Teaming a Sovereign LLM, Its Reasoning and Its Training Stages

abstract: While numerous studies have focused on multivariate time series anomaly detection, many existing methods perform poorly or are not directly applicable to univariate settings. We introduce FourStat, a dual-model framework for univariate time series anomaly detection that combines two complementary approaches. The Fourier Autoencoder (FAE) captures global patterns like seasonality through frequency-domain analysis, while the Stationary Autoencoder (SAE) focuses on local structures by enforcing statistical stationarity. We also propose a new evaluation metric called Perfect Point that assesses whether perfect F1-scores can be achieved directly from anomaly scores, eliminating thresholding subjectivity. Results demonstrate that FourStat outperforms existing baselines, particularly on challenging anomaly types, while the new metric provides clearer insights into model performance gaps and advantages.
title: FourStat: A Dual AutoEncoder Leveraging Frequency and Stationarity for Time Series Anomaly Detection

abstract: A small ground robot can carry one camera and a few watts of compute, but the depth foundation models that could turn that camera into a range sensor are vision transformers sized for GPUs. We bring one to a Raspberry Pi 5 with the Hailo-8L, an accelerator that runs every layer in integer arithmetic, attention included. Quantised for it, Depth Anything V2 loses large parts of the scene, and we measure why: at 449 tokens, 91% of softmax weights fall below one int8 step while carrying 17-33% of the attention mass. Our answer is to distil, not quantise. An attention-free ResNet-34 U-Net student of Depth Anything V2-Large (24.5M parameters) runs at 27.1 FPS on the chip, its int8 output matches its float twin (Pearson 0.99993), and on held-out scenes of its simulated yard it is the most accurate depth network on the chip (AbsRel 0.269 against 0.354-0.530). On 1,000 stereo-verified points of a real outdoor drive it is not resolvably different from the vendor's Depth Anything V2-Small build, while running faster (27.1 vs 21.6 FPS). Ranging obstacles by where they meet the floor needs only the camera height, so mapping, hybrid-A* planning and SLAM run on the Pi's own CPU. In real-time hardware-in-the-loop tests in a Gaussian-splat reconstruction of a real yard, the stack reaches the goal without contact in 7.9$\pm$1.1 of 10 scenes, against 9.2$\pm$0.4 with exact obstacles, and in 7.7$\pm$0.7 on its own pose with simulated wheel odometry (ten seeds each; 8.2$\pm$0.4 with the real Pi and Hailo-8L in the loop, five seeds). The source code, pre-trained models and data are available at https://github.com/itaim18/DANIEL.
title: Seeing to Drive on a Single Board: Attention-Free Depth for Onboard Robot Navigation

abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs) distribute reasoning across specialized agents that must exchange messages and invoke tools reliably. Existing evaluations typically couple communication with open domain tasks, making it difficult to determine whether a failure arises from reasoning, malformed tool use, lost messages, or forgotten requests. Prior benchmarks do not isolate communication execution or measure routing redundancy against a known optimal path. We introduce CypherMAS, a synthetic benchmark that isolates communication and routing in fixed multi-agent graphs. Agents in chain, star, bipartite, or ring graphs route cyphered messages to remote peers holding the matching decoders; since the optimal route is known, redundant LLM calls can be measured and routing failures may be easily tracked. Across eleven open-weight models from 4B to 753B, small models fail at routing and tool use, dense models above 27B degrade with diameter, and successful runs exceed minimum LLM calls. These findings identify communication reliability as a distinct scaling bottleneck for multi-agent systems and provide a controlled diagnostic for complex multi-agent systems. The source code is freely available: https://github.com/Andoree/CypherMAS.
title: CypherMAS: Benchmarking Routing Reliability in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at medical question answering yet are rarely evaluated on the stepwise diagnostic reasoning that defines real clinical workflows, where impressions are revised as information accumulates. We build Annotated Stepwise Clinical rEasoning for NaturalisTic Diagnosis (ASCENT), a clinician-annotated benchmark and training resource of 3,078 stepwise problems derived from MedQA-USMLE that decomposes each vignette into EMR-aligned steps (Findings, Impression, supporting Rationale), enabling evaluation of intermediate reasoning under incomplete information. Experiments and training with ASCENT revealed insights into how current LLMs handle stepwise diagnostic reasoning. Even strong reasoning models that perform well on MedQA-USMLE leave substantial headroom on ASCENT, and general-purpose frontier models trail further, exposing a persistent gap between fully informed and stepwise diagnosis. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-7B and 32B on ASCENT yields measurable F1 gains over both pre-trained and HuatuoGPT-o1 CoT-trained baselines, with gains driven primarily by precision. Complementary robustness analyses (counterfactual perturbation, format-vs-content control, judge agreement, and rollout) further show that ASCENT-fine-tuned models rely on the diagnostic content of prior impressions rather than imitating their output format, while error propagation under rollout remains a key challenge for clinical deployment.
title: ASCENT: A Benchmark for Evaluating and Advancing Stepwise Diagnostic Reasoning in Large Language Models on Common Clinical Scenarios

abstract: Community detection offers an alternative to conventional methods for data analysis tasks such as feature selection and clustering, and detecting communities with quantum algorithms is a promising avenue for quantum speedup. We investigate quantum spectral community detectors, such as the modularity-matrix algorithm deteQt, in pipelines for both tasks. We first generalise deteQt to multiple communities by recursive bisection, and show that it recovers planted communities, and hence redundant features, in synthetic and small datasets. We then propose projeQt, which applies a spectral filter to the encoded modularity matrix through the quantum singular value transformation, retaining higher-order eigenvectors that deteQt does not use. projeQt acts on the generalised modularity matrix and extracts several communities at once, without recursion, by k-means clustering of a Gram matrix built from quantum state overlaps. On MNIST we demonstrate both pipelines, selecting informative pixels and classifying images directly by clustering, and find them competitive with standard community detectors.
title: Quantum Community Detection for Data Analysis

abstract: Machine Learning (ML) models are already being deployed at scale for malware detection. Therefore there is a pressing need to rigorously study adversarial robustness. To that end, we introduce the Adversarial AI Engine (AAIE): a platform for automated security stress-testing. We performed transfer attacks, via EMBER2018, against a Random Forest target. Counterintuitively, we found single-step FGSM to have the highest attack success rate (ASR) of 52.9% compared to iterative PGD with 45.2% (p < 0.002). Compared to iterative attacks which tend to overfit surrogate networks creating brittle perturbations, FGSM created more transferable examples. We benchmarked our attacks using ASR, transferability score, evasion rate, and resilience index. Through these metrics, proposed in concordance with emerging standards in AI governance, we expose shortcomings as our transferability scores peak at ~0.8 with constrained perturbations. We highlight the practical security implications of these findings and demonstrate AAIE for automated adversarial auditing.
title: Beyond the Efficiency-Efficacy Dilemma: A Critical Analysis of Transferability in Adversarial Malware Detection

abstract: Simple cellular automata (CAs) can be computationally universal, but their rules are designed by hand. We train Neural Cellular Automata (NCAs), which learn a local update rule by gradient descent, to compute exact digital logic. Bits are encoded as clusters of cells on a 2D grid, and a result reaches the output only by propagating through intermediate cells. One model is trained per task: logic gates, 4- and 8-bit ripple-carry adders, and a preliminary 8-bit arithmetic logic unit (ALU). All gate and adder models reach 100% bit correctness in 10 of 10 seeds, and exhaustive tests over all input pairs find at most 1 error in 256 (4-bit) and 7 in 65,536 (8-bit). Adders trained on operands of up to 3 bits generalize to 8 bits. The adders propagate the carry as a wave, with a delay of about 3.5 steps per bit of the carry chain. Outputs are correct only within the trained rollout length.
title: NCPU: Towards Cell-Inspired Spatial Computing
